extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, foundations of mathematics, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for how to form, justify, and evaluate hypotheses, definitions, and axioms in mathematical and empirical sciences, with emphasis on geometry and the evidence for first principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of simplifying hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: For scientific convenience we may treat objects as divested of all properties except those material to our purpose (feign them to be divested of other properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is permissible to neglect nonessential physical properties or irregularities when they have no practical effect on the result. Such simplifications are legitimate only if one remains aware they are fictions introduced for convenience and restores neglected properties whenever their presence or absence would materially affect the truth of conclusions. Example: treat bodies as purely geometrical figures unless material properties (like thermal expansion) alter the conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses must relate to real existence
rubrics_metrics.description: An hypothesis for scientific inquiry must relate to something which has real existence; science cannot legitimately be about nonentities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses may exaggerate or suppress certain real properties but must not ascribe to the thing any property which it has not. One's liberty is limited to small exaggerations or suppressions that can be corrected; arbitrary hypotheses about nonexisting things yield only intellectual exercises, not additions to knowledge of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of conclusions is relative to assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'necessity' of geometrical (or deductive) conclusions consists only in that they correctly follow from the suppositions from which they are deduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusions of any deductive science are necessary only insofar as they legitimately follow from unexamined assumptions (the inductions or hypotheses). Therefore calling conclusions 'necessary truths' presupposes the premises are accepted for the purposes of the inquiry; it does not make the premises themselves necessary or true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between definitions/hypotheses and axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Some first principles involved in definitions are hypotheses (conventional simplifications), while axioms are general propositions that may be true without hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions often introduce idealized objects (e.g., straight lines) by supposing certain properties; these are hypotheses useful for deduction. By contrast, certain axioms (e.g., magnitudes equal to the same are equal to one another) are viewed as true of real objects without mixture of hypothesis. Evaluations should distinguish which foundational principles are definitional fictions and which are empirical generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible definitions must correspond to conceivably frameable conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition, to be admissible, must refer to and agree with some conception which we can distinctly frame in our thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions should not be purely arbitrary: the defined terms must map onto ideas or representations we can form. Example (from Whewell): definitions of straight lines must match the conception by which we identify angles, parallelism, and bounded triangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some axioms are indemonstrable fundamental truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Among axioms there exist a few fundamental truths not capable of demonstration (e.g., two straight lines that coincide in two points coincide altogether).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some axioms can be rephrased as definitions or shown by constructions, certain basic geometric truths must be taken as primitive. Recognize which axioms are demonstrable and which must be accepted as primitive postulates when building a deductive system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms as experimental generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms are experimental truths—generalizations from observation—rather than purely a priori revelations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The belief in axioms (e.g., 'two straight lines cannot enclose a space') can be grounded in repeated observation and mental experimentation. The page argues that axioms receive their force from empirical regularities and our capacity to form accurate mental images that reflect real objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental images as legitimate basis for geometric evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental pictures (imaginary intuition) can serve as subjects of geometrical experimentation because ideas of form resemble sensations and faithfully represent prototypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because mental diagrams can reproduce the properties of real figures 'with a distinctness equal to reality', reasoning about them may legitimately stand in for empirical observation in geometry—provided we have prior experience that mental images reliably represent reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceivability does not establish necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The inconceivableness of the negation of a proposition does not prove that the proposition rests on evidence beyond experience, because conceivability depends on habit and mental association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (antipodes, Newtonian gravity) show that what earlier thinkers found inconceivable later became conceivable and true. Thus using the current inability to imagine a counter-case as proof of metaphysical necessity is fallacious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of empirical proof (infinite extension) overcome by imagination combined with experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Although observation cannot extend to infinity (e.g., to show two lines never meet), imagination—backed by experience of how straightness appears—allows us to infer the axiom's truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We cannot observe lines to infinity, but mental transport to hypothetical distant points and the learned equivalence of mental pictures and real objects justify conclusions about unobservable continuations, so long as the mental representations have been validated by experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximations acceptable when corrections are known
rubrics_metrics.description: Many scientific propositions are approximations to truth; we may 'feign' exactness for use, provided we know the liability to correction and can restore neglected factors when they materially affect results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: treating the earth's figure as spherical when small departures exist, or ignoring material properties in geometry until they become relevant. Scientific practice accepts approximate axioms where they facilitate deduction and where compensatory corrections can be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological origin of conviction in axioms (association and habit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our conviction that some propositions are necessary often arises from long-continued association and habit of thought, not from intrinsic a priori insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because strong associative habits can render certain negations inconceivable, evaluators should examine whether 'necessity' is psychological (habit-based) rather than metaphysical. Training and exposure can alter what is conceivable; thus historical contingency matters in assessing claims about necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that scientific hypotheses be open to correction
rubrics_metrics.description: When hypotheses simplify reality, there is an 'indispensable obligation' to restore suppressed properties whenever their inclusion would materially change conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit procedural norm: intentionally idealized assumptions must be treated as provisional and updated when their omission causes significant error. Anti-pattern: treating idealizations as literal truths and failing to apply corrections when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish demonstrable axioms from those captured by definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some axioms can be recast as definitions or proven by constructions (e.g., certain equalities via superposition), while others remain foundational and non-demonstrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In building or evaluating a deductive system, identify which principles are eliminable (convertible to definitions or derivable) and which must be preserved as primitive axioms; choose primitives that minimize arbitrary assumptions yet suffice for desired deductions.
